items.title: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe by an estimated 5 °C
items.claim: How much does ocean circulation warm western Europe?

options.text: Not at all — climate is determined by latitude alone

Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) and modelling studies suggest the wider North Atlantic circulation system contributes around 5-10 °C of additional warmth to western Europe
By 30 °C — without it Europe would be like Antarctica

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it broadens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the heat onshore.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that atmospheric heat transport and the southwesterly stationary wave (set up by the Rocky Mountains) are at least as important as ocean heat in distinguishing western from eastern continental winters. The single-cause 'Gulf Stream warms Britain' story is too simple.

The AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021). A collapse would cool Europe and warm the tropics.
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems acting together. The Gulf Stream story is partly true and partly simplified; a teaching answer needs both the ocean and the atmosphere.

items.title: Major volcanic eruptions inject ash into the stratosphere
items.claim: How high can a large eruption column reach?

options.text: Up to 5 km — high but contained in the troposphere
Plinian eruptions can exceed 30-40 km, well into the stratosphere — Mount Pinatubo (1991) reached around 35 km
Only the visible smoke is observable
No eruption has reached the stratosphere in recorded history

items.reveal:
Plinian eruptions (named after Pliny the Younger's description of Vesuvius in 79 CE) drive ash and sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere, where they can spread globally and remain for years. Pinatubo (June 1991) cooled global temperatures by around 0.5°C for 18 months.

Tambora (1815, VEI 7) caused the 'Year Without a Summer' (1816) — crop failures across Europe and North America, snow in June. Krakatoa (1883, VEI 6) produced spectacular sunsets globally. Toba (around 74,000 years ago, VEI 8) may have caused a population bottleneck in early humans.
items.why: Volcanic forcing is one of the strongest natural climate drivers on year-to-decade scales. Climate models calibrate against these events because the signal is large and well-dated.

items.title: Coral reefs fix nitrogen and support a quarter of marine species
items.claim: What is the ecological importance of coral reefs?

options.text: They are aesthetic features with little ecological role

Reefs cover under 0.1% of the ocean floor but host around 25% of marine species; symbiotic cyanobacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, fertilising nutrient-poor tropical waters; reefs also protect coasts from wave energy
Reefs are made entirely of dead material
Reefs occur only in polar oceans

items.reveal:
Reefs occupy around 284,000 km² globally — under 0.1% of the ocean — and yet host an estimated 4,000 fish species, 800 reef-building coral species, and uncounted invertebrates.

Cyanobacteria in coral tissues and on reef surfaces fix atmospheric nitrogen, providing essential nutrients in otherwise oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) tropical waters. The reefs function as 'oases' of productivity.

Mass bleaching events (1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2024) have hit major systems. The Great Barrier Reef has bleached in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Estimated coastal protection value is tens of billions of dollars annually.
items.why: Concentrated biodiversity means concentrated risk. Losing reefs means losing entire ecosystems — not just iconic species — and removing coastal protection from hundreds of millions of people.
